title: Anthropic replaced Git with Scion after scaling to 30k daily commits
content:
Anthropic Just Broke Software’s Most Proven Tool: Why AI Blasts Your Pipelines
Anthropic ditched Git after merges surged 12x from AI agents. The lesson: before scaling AI, find out which operational pipe in your business will burst.
(🇪🇸 Leer la versión en español aquí)
The Myth: The Fantasy of Frictionless Productivity
A remarkably profitable myth currently dominates executive boardrooms and operational committees: the belief that implementing artificial intelligence is as simple as buying enterprise subscriptions, handing out seats, and watching performance climb magically with zero friction.
We are told that AI is a clean drop-in accelerator. That if a department used to take days to draft reports or resolve client disputes, clicking a button will instantly 10x throughput without touching existing processes or backend wiring.
It is a comfortable, seductive story. It is also dead wrong.
Production reality in the trenches is far more unyielding: AI does not fix operational friction; it exposes it by multiplying volume. When you crank up work volume tenfold or a hundredfold without widening the pipes carrying that data, your organization does not become agile: it chokes.
The clearest demonstration of this systemic shock did not happen in a legacy brick-and-mortar office, but right inside the engine room of one of the world's premier frontier AI labs: Anthropic.
The Real Problem: The Anthropic Lesson
A few days ago, Anthropic's engineering team—the architects behind the Claude model family—published an eye-opening architectural report with an astonishing admission: they had to abandon Git, the undisputed universal standard on which nearly all modern software has been built for the last two decades.
Their decision was not driven by aesthetic preferences or developer vanity. It was dictated by the raw physics of distributed systems.
In May 2026, Anthropic engineers were merging roughly 2,500 code changes per day into their central monorepo—a solid, healthy figure for a fast-growing tech company. By September 2026, barely four months later, that volume skyrocketed past 30,000 changes per day.
A staggering 12x surge in daily throughput.
That avalanche did not come from aggressive hiring or developers drinking triple espressos. Humans were no longer writing the code: thousands of autonomous AI agents were generating, testing, and shipping code in parallel around the clock.
Faced with that relentless algorithmic tsunami, the most battle-tested developer tool on Earth buckled under pressure.
The Analogy: The Notary and the Ten Thousand Couriers
To see why the tooling broke without getting bogged down in low-level developer syntax, think of a traditional notary office.
Picture Git as a meticulous notary sitting behind a registry desk with an official ledger. Whenever an employee completes a company document, they walk over to the notary's counter. The notary reviews the draft, ensures no one else modified the same paragraph simultaneously, stamps it with a heavy brass seal, logs the exact timestamp, and archives it.
When an organization has 50 human employees visiting the counter two or three times a day, this workflow is a masterpiece of reliability. Every employee keeps a local copy of their dossiers on their personal desk, works offline without latency, and only calls on the notary when the document is ready for official sign-off. For twenty years, this sequential, human-centric model ruled the software world.
Now imagine replacing those 50 employees with 10,000 hyper-fast automated couriers delivering documents at the exact same second.
Suddenly, thousands of mechanical couriers shove millions of pages into the registry slot simultaneously. The notary cannot physically lift the brass stamp fast enough. The waiting line wraps three times around the city block. Hallways jam under tons of paper, the telephone switchboard melts down, and the entire office grinds to a dead halt.
That is precisely what happened to Git. It was designed in 2005 by Linus Torvalds for human developers working on laptops with intermittent connectivity, not for a synthetic army hammering servers with 25 million checkout requests daily and generating over 600 petabytes of saturated network traffic. The human-scale registry choked on machine-scale volume.
The Solution: Building an Industrial Pipeline from Scratch
When an old pipe bursts from extreme hydraulic pressure, applying duct tape is futile. Anthropic could not simply throw beefier servers at the problem. They assigned a tight team of seven engineers for five months to engineer an entirely custom, agent-native version control platform named Scion.
Scion abandons the offline notary model completely:
- It assumes client agents are always online.
- Instead of forcing every agent to clone nearly 100 gigabytes of historical dead weight, changes are managed virtually and incrementally on the central server.
- Continuous validation runs in seconds rather than minutes.
The production numbers speak for themselves: Scion uses 200 times fewer CPU and memory resources than the legacy Git mirroring architecture, cutting checkout bottlenecks down to seconds and freeing up 25% of their CI infrastructure capacity. They had to build an entirely new industrial pipeline because the old one disintegrated under machine throughput.
The Business Impact: Where Your Operations Will Crack
It is tempting for business leaders to brush this off as an exotic anecdote about Silicon Valley coders playing with internal scripts. That is a dangerous misjudgment.
Code is simply structured information. What happened to Anthropic's version control is a direct preview of the operational whiplash waiting for any traditional business that rolls out AI without upgrading its foundational pipes:
- Sales and Outbound: If an AI agent generates 10x more qualified sales leads every morning, but your sales team can only physically make twenty calls a day, you have not accelerated revenue. You have created an unmanageable backlog of decaying leads and burned out your account executives.
- Customer Support: If an AI model categorizes and answers customer inquiries at lightning speed, but every resolution requires manual approval inside a legacy ERP or an overloaded shared spreadsheet, the spreadsheet corrupts, the database locks up, and customers receive meaningless auto-replies.
- Procurement and Logistics: If automated algorithms optimize restock orders every five minutes, but your physical loading dock only has bays for three trucks, incoming delivery gridlock paralyzes the distribution center.
AI is a jet engine. Bolting a jet engine onto the chassis of a delivery bicycle does not give you a supersonic aircraft; it leaves a trail of twisted metal along the highway.
The primary bottleneck in enterprise productivity has never been the speed of generating content, leads, or proposals. The true bottleneck is the physical throughput capacity of your operational channels to absorb, validate, and execute that volume.
The Final Question
The true existential threat AI poses to your bottom line has nothing to do with sci-fi rebellions or rogue algorithms. The real danger is mundane and immediate: operational strangulation by pure volume.
Before your leadership team signs the next software contract or kicks off another automation pilot, shift your technical focus:
Before adopting AI, ask yourself which operational pipeline in your company will burst when volume multiplies by 10.

report.summary: Anthropic reportedly replaced Git with custom agent-native Scion after AI-driven merge volume surged 12x to 30,000 daily commits, exposing operational bottlenecks.
report.background: Git was created in 2005 for human developers working on laptops, with full local clones, offline work, and sequential review. That model works well at human scale but strains when autonomous AI agents generate, test, and merge code in parallel around the clock. According to the report, Anthropic's monorepo grew from roughly 2,500 daily merges in May 2026 to more than 30,000 by September 2026. The bottleneck was not code generation but the version-control and CI plumbing needed to validate and absorb the volume. The episode reflects a broader industry pattern: agentic AI can multiply throughput faster than existing engineering and business processes can adapt.
key_points: Anthropic's merge volume rose from about 2,500 to over 30,000 changes per day in four months, a 12x surge. The report attributes this to thousands of autonomous AI agents generating and shipping code in parallel, not to aggressive hiring or ordinary developer productivity gains.

Git's human-scale design became the constraint. The article says Anthropic's workload produced tens of millions of daily checkout requests and hundreds of petabytes of network traffic, while full clones of roughly 100GB of history and sequential validation choked under machine-speed parallel demand.

Anthropic built Scion, an agent-native version-control platform, with a small team over five months. It assumes agents are always online, manages changes incrementally and virtually on the central server, avoids full historical clones, and runs continuous validation in seconds rather than minutes.

The reported results are dramatic: Scion uses far fewer CPU and memory resources than the legacy Git mirroring setup, cuts checkout bottlenecks to seconds, and frees about 25% of CI capacity. The lesson is that AI productivity gains can expose and overwhelm downstream infrastructure.

The broader warning extends beyond software. If AI multiplies leads, support tickets, or restock orders without expanding approval, ERP, sales, or logistics capacity, organizations get backlogs, lockups, and burnout rather than faster operations.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the Anthropic case makes platform engineering a strategic priority: agent-native version control, CI scheduling, validation, observability, and rate limiting may matter as much as model quality. Developers should watch monorepo tooling, sparse checkouts, server-side changesets, and stacked-diff workflows; most teams need not abandon Git immediately, but high-volume agent workflows will stress it. For regular users, AI features may arrive faster, yet the visible experience will depend on whether organizations expand review and approval capacity. The real risk is operational strangulation: AI accelerates generation, but bottlenecks move to validation, execution, and human sign-off.
report.tools: Watch Anthropic Engineering's Scion write-up for architecture ideas, though Scion appears internal rather than a drop-in product. Compare concepts with Git sparse checkout and LFS, Jujutsu, Sapling, Gerrit, and Perforce for large monorepos. Also evaluate CI queue observability, agent orchestration, and automated validation tools. The practical takeaway is to test where your pipeline breaks under 10x volume before adopting more AI automation.
